Mitigate

MIT-uh-gayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To mitigate is to make something harmful, serious, or severe less so.

Building codes now require new homes in flood zones to include features that mitigate water damage during storms.

Worked Example

Negotiators worked through the night hoping a partial agreement might mitigate the damage of a full-blown trade war.

Mitigate means to lessen the severity of harm -- it doesn't necessarily make a bad situation good, just less bad.

How Mitigate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

lessen

lessen: to make smaller or less severe

relieve

relieve: to make pain, harm, or difficulty less intense

Antonyms

worsen

worsen: to make or become worse

intensify

intensify: to make something stronger or more severe

How Strong Is It? — ease → mitigate → eliminate

ease vs. mitigate

ease vs. mitigate: Ease means to make something a little less severe or uncomfortable, a milder change than mitigate.

eliminate vs. mitigate

eliminate vs. mitigate: Eliminate means to remove something completely, a far more total fix than merely mitigating it.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — mit-

root — mit-: mild, gentle (Latin mitis, 'mild')

suffix — -igate

suffix — -igate: to make (Latin -igare)

Put it together

Put it together: Mitigate comes from Latin mitis ('mild or gentle') + -igare ('to make') -- literally 'to make mild.' English 'mild' itself comes from a different, Germanic root, so this Latin root doesn't survive elsewhere in common English.

Use the root in a new word: mitigation

Use the root in a new word: mitigation: The city's flood mitigation plan included new drainage tunnels and higher levees.
